common_name: Madame Francis Mango (Francis Mango, Haitian Dessert Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Madame Francis is one of the earliest-ripening mangos in South Florida, often producing more than one flush of fruit per year.

directions: Madame Francis is the signature dooryard and commercial mango of Haiti, where it is grown at vast scale for both domestic eating and export. The polyembryonic, oblong-kidney-shaped fruit turns solid bright yellow at full ripeness, with fiberless to lightly fibrous orange flesh and an intensely rich, sweet flavor that holds up well even when the tree is pushed with heavy nitrogen. The open, vigorous tree carries large, light green leaves and shows better anthracnose tolerance than many older Florida cultivars, letting it crop reliably through humid early summer. Expect fruit to ripen earlier than most other mangos in a home orchard, often starting in June, and withhold irrigation as fruit matures to concentrate sugars.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun; Mallika stays compact enough for small dooryard lots and containers compared to most Indian-type mangos.

directions: Mallika was bred at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute in New Delhi by crossing the classic Indian cultivars Neelum and Dasheri, pairing Neelum's late, heat-tolerant cropping with Dasheri's rich flavor. The oblong, flattened fruit ripens canary-yellow often blushed pink, with fiberless flesh carrying pronounced citrus, melon, and honey notes that make it one of the most intensely flavored dessert mangos grown in Florida. Grafted trees stay naturally smaller and more precocious than most Indian-type mangos, making Mallika a favorite for growers with limited space who still want a heavy-bearing, disease-resistant tree. Pick fruit mature-green and ripen it at room temperature in a closed box for the best eating quality.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with ample room, or commit to annual pruning to keep this naturally large tree manageable in a home yard.

directions: Lancetilla originated from a Saigon x Mulgoba cross grown by plant explorer Wilson Popenoe on Honduras's north coast and was later popularized in South Florida after a strong showing at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden's mango festival. It is prized for producing some of the largest fiberless mango fruit grown in home gardens, regularly averaging around two pounds and occasionally reaching five, with red-blushed skin wrapped around sweet, lemon-yellow flesh. The tree is notably vigorous and disease-resistant, but left unpruned it grows quite large, so plan on a big planting site or an annual pruning regimen to keep it at dooryard scale. Give it full sun, well-drained soil, and frost protection while young, since mango wood of any cultivar is easily damaged by cold.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun; Rosigold stays low and can be pruned to hold around 8 feet, making it a good choice for small lots and containers.

directions: Rosigold was selected in South Florida from Southeast Asian mango heritage and later analysis traced it to a seedling of the Ono cultivar, but it is best known today as one of the earliest-ripening mangos grown in home gardens, with fruit maturing as early as March and April. The oblong, under-a-pound fruit turns yellow with an occasional orange-red blush and carries fiberless, orange-yellow flesh with a rich, sweet flavor well ahead of the main mango season. Its naturally low growth habit, which holds easily to about eight feet with routine pruning, makes it a popular pick for growers who want an early crop without a towering tree. Grow it like other mangos, in full sun with excellent drainage, and reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate sweetness.

common_name: Carabao Mango (Philippine Mango, Manila Super Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Carabao is polyembryonic like other Southeast Asian mangos, so seedlings largely come true, but a grafted selection ripens faster and truer to type.

directions: Carabao is the signature mango of the Philippines, named for the water buffalo that is the country's national animal, and ranks among the sweetest mangos grown anywhere. The kidney-shaped fruit ripens to bright yellow with rich, fiberless, deep-yellow flesh that carries an intensely sweet, floral, honey-like flavor and strong aroma. Like other Southeast Asian mango types it is polyembryonic, so seed-grown trees are usually true to type, but grafted trees fruit sooner and more predictably in a home orchard setting. Grow it in full sun with excellent drainage, protect young wood from any frost, and ease off irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to build sugar.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Branca is identified by its bright green, rather than purple-black, ripe fruit, so harvest by size and give rather than skin darkening.

directions: Branca stands apart from most jaboticaba selections in that its fruit ripens to a bright, translucent green rather than the usual deep purple-black, which can make a first harvest feel surprising to growers expecting typical jaboticaba color. The medium-to-large fruit is flavorful and the tree is a heavy, reliable producer once established, bearing the same trunk-borne clusters characteristic of the species. Culture matches other jaboticaba cultivars: full sun, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and consistent moisture, since the shallow root system does not tolerate extended drought. Protect young trees from temperatures below the upper 20s F, and judge ripeness on Branca by fruit size and slight softening rather than relying on color change.
sources: Purdue University Horticulture — Jaboticabas (Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)

common_name: Pingo de Mel Jaboticaba (Honey Drop Jaboticaba)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Pingo de Mel is a Sabara-type selection grown for eating quality rather than fruit size, so site it for easy fresh snacking access near the trunk.

directions: Pingo de Mel, meaning drop of honey in Portuguese, is a modern Brazilian selection made by screening thousands of seedling trees at a large jaboticaba estate in Goias state for exceptional sweetness and thin skin, and it has since become one of the most widely planted jaboticaba selections in Brazil. The fruit resembles the classic Sabara type in size and habit but eats noticeably sweeter and less acidic, with thin skin and a high ratio of juicy pulp to seed that lets whole fruit be eaten out of hand with little waste. The tree flushes its trunk-borne purple-black fruit in the same concentrated bursts typical of Sabara-type jaboticabas, several times a year once mature. Grow it like other jaboticaba cultivars, in full sun on fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with reliable moisture, and shelter young trees from temperatures below the upper 20s F.
